Step 1: Creating the Complex Class
Our first step is to create a Complex class that contains:

items: variables (called attributes in OOP) to store the real and imaginary parts of the complex number
overloaded operators that perform the necessary calculations
a member function (also known as a method in OOP) to display the results

blocks.content: First, let's just create a skeleton of the class without adding any functionality to the overloaded operators:
Let's look at the above code in greater detail.
1. Member Variables (Attributes)
The double variables real and imag store the real and imaginary parts of a complex number, respectively. They are private and are thus inaccessible outside the class.
2. Constructors
Notice that we have used two constructors: one without parameters i.e. a default constructor, and the other with two parameters real and imag.
Here's what the two constructors do:

items: Default Constructor - sets the values of both member variables to 0.0.
Parameterized Constructor - sets the values of the member variables to those of its parameters.

blocks.content: It's important to note that the real and imag parameters are different from the attributes we've defined in the class.
To avoid confusion, we have used the this pointer to refer to the member variables i.e. inside the parameterized constructor:

items: this->real and this->imag refer to member variables of the Complex class
real and imag refer to the arguments passed to the constructor of the Complex class

blocks.content: Outside the parameterized constructor, real and imag will refer to the member variables again, unless specified otherwise.
3. Overloaded Operators
We have overloaded the +, -, *, and / operators to perform the calculations. These operators are binary operators i.e. they take two operands.
So, we advise you to revise the lesson on Binary Operator Overloading if you're not confident in your knowledge.
4. Member Function (Method)
Finally, we have declared a method named get_result() to return the result (in string format) of the calculation.
Next, we'll add functionality to the overloaded operator() functions.
